common_name: Aeranthos Air Plant (Cobalt Air Plant, Argentine Tillandsia)

planting.note: Mount on bark, wire, or a rock in bright indirect to gentle direct sun; Tillandsia aeranthos is epiphytic and grows with no soil, clumping outward from short rhizomes into dense mats that can be left outdoors year-round in zone 9-11.

directions: Tillandsia aeranthos is a clumping, rhizomatous air plant from Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil that branches from the base into low mounds rather than staying single-rosetted like most air plants in this collection. Slender, silvery-green leaves surround short flower stalks tipped with rose-pink bracts and vivid cobalt-blue to violet flowers that open in succession over several weeks. It tolerates brief cool nights better than many tropical tillandsias and is often grown lashed to rocks or driftwood where its clumping habit forms an attractive spreading colony over a few seasons. Water by misting or dunking two to three times weekly and let dry within a few hours to avoid rot at the base of the clump.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia aeranthos cultivation notes

planting.note: Mount on mesquite, oak bark, or a fence rail in bright, mostly sunny exposure; this South Texas native air plant tolerates more direct sun and brief dry spells than most Tillandsia and needs no soil.

directions: Tillandsia baileyi is native to the brushlands of the lower Rio Grande Valley of South Texas and northeastern Mexico, where it grows on mesquite and huisache in full exposure to intense heat and sun. Its narrow, channeled, silver-gray leaves curl and reflex backward into a bulbous, twisting base, giving the plant a windswept, almost sculptural look distinct from the tighter bulbous form of T. bulbosa or the rosette of T. ionantha. Rose-red bracts hold small violet flowers in spring. Because it comes from a semi-arid native range, it is more sun- and drought-tolerant than tropical rainforest tillandsias and appreciates less frequent misting.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Native Tillandsia of South Texas
Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia baileyi species profile

planting.note: Mount on bark or driftwood in bright indirect to filtered direct light; the rush-like leaves need no soil and benefit from good airflow between waterings.

directions: Tillandsia juncea forms an upright tuft of thin, wiry, cylindrical, rush-like leaves that give the plant a grass- or reed-textured silhouette entirely unlike the flattened or bulbous leaf forms of most tillandsias already in this collection. Ranging from Mexico through Central America into South America, it produces a slender spike of pink to red bracts with small violet-blue flowers at the tips of its clustered stems. Its narrow, almost needle-like foliage makes it a useful textural contrast plant in mixed mounted air plant displays. Water by misting or brief dunking two to three times a week and allow the tight leaf bases to dry fully to prevent rot.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia juncea cultivation

planting.note: Mount on bark in bright, filtered shade; velvety leaf surfaces trap and hold moisture longer than glossy-leaved tillandsias, so allow extra drying time between waterings to avoid rot.

directions: Tillandsia velutina is distinguished by densely fuzzy, velvet-textured leaves covered in fine trichomes, giving the whole plant a soft, matte appearance quite different from the smoother or scaly foliage of T. ionantha or T. bulbosa already in this collection. In bright light the compact rosette flushes a deep, saturated red from base to tip, one of the most vivid color changes among small blushing tillandsias, before producing a short spike of violet flowers. Native to the forests of southern Mexico and Central America, it grows as a true epiphyte on tree branches in filtered light. Because the velvety leaf texture slows evaporation, misting slightly less often than smooth-leaved species helps prevent basal rot.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia velutina species profile

planting.note: Mount on bark or a slab in bright, filtered shade; this understory epiphyte needs no soil and prefers higher humidity with regular misting rather than harsh direct sun.

directions: Tillandsia multicaulis takes its name from its habit of producing multiple flattened, sword-like flower spikes simultaneously from a single broad rosette of soft green leaves, unlike the single-spiked bloom of most tillandsias in this collection. The overlapping bracts along each spike shade from yellow-green at the base to bright red at the tip, framing small violet flowers, and the multi-stemmed display can persist for weeks. Native to cloud forests from Mexico to Colombia, it grows as a shaded epiphyte and appreciates more humidity and less direct sun than desert-adapted tillandsias like T. xerographica. Mist regularly and provide good airflow to prevent the broader leaf bases from staying wet too long.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia multicaulis species profile

planting.note: Mount on bark in bright, filtered shade with high humidity; this rare Ecuadorian epiphyte grows slowly with no soil and benefits from frequent misting rather than direct sun exposure.

directions: Tillandsia dyeriana is a rare, slow-growing epiphyte from the coastal fog forests of western Ecuador, prized for a torch-like inflorescence of glowing orange bracts that rises well above the soft, light-green, strap-shaped foliage — a brighter, more saturated orange than the reds and pinks typical of other tillandsias in this collection. The bracts hold small yellow flowers and remain colorful for many weeks, making mature specimens a striking focal point in a shaded epiphyte display. Because its native habitat receives near-constant moisture from coastal fog, it appreciates more frequent misting and higher humidity than dry-forest species like T. xerographica or T. duratii. Its slow growth and limited native range make it a more premium, specialty air plant.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia dyeriana species profile

planting.note: Hang loosely or drape over a branch in bright, mostly sunny exposure; the tendril-like leaves are adapted to actively coil around twigs for support and need no soil or fixed mounting.

directions: Tillandsia duratii is immediately recognizable by its long, silvery, curling leaves that spiral and coil like tendrils to actively grasp surrounding branches in its native dry forests of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Brazil — a self-anchoring habit unlike the straight or reflexed foliage of other tillandsias here. In bloom, it produces a dense head of lavender-blue, strongly fragrant flowers emerging from pale green bracts, among the more noticeably scented tillandsia blooms. Because it comes from semi-arid habitats, it tolerates brighter sun and less frequent watering than tropical rainforest species. It is often displayed loosely draped rather than firmly mounted so the curling leaves can express their natural coiling form.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia duratii species profile

planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright light with some direct morning sun; the dense coating of trichomes makes this species more drought-tolerant than most air plants and needs no soil.

directions: Tillandsia albida forms an elongated, tubular rosette of narrow leaves so densely covered in white trichome scales that the entire plant appears frosted or powdery, a more pronounced silver-white coating than the silvery-green tone of T. bergeri or T. tectorum. This heavy scale layer is an adaptation to the arid scrublands of Mexico where it grows in intense sun and reflects excess light while capturing atmospheric moisture. It sends up a tall, slender spike of pink bracts with small blue-violet flowers. Because of its drought adaptation, it tolerates brighter sun and less frequent misting than most epiphytic tillandsias and is prone to rot if watered too often.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia albida species profile

planting.note: Mount on bark in bright, filtered shade with high humidity; the heavily fuzzed leaves are prone to rot if kept wet too long, so ensure good airflow and quick drying after misting.

directions: Tillandsia pruinosa forms a small, bulbous, turnip-shaped base of curling, gray-green leaves so thickly covered in fuzzy white trichomes that the whole plant looks frosted or powdered, a coarser and denser fuzz than the smoother scales of T. bulbosa. It grows as a true epiphyte in humid cloud forests from Mexico through Central America into northern South America, typically nestled in mossy tree crevices in dappled shade. Rose-colored bracts hold small violet flowers in a compact spike close to the leaves. Because the dense trichome layer slows drying, it is especially prone to basal rot if watered too frequently, so err on the side of less frequent misting with excellent airflow.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia pruinosa species profile

planting.note: Mount on bark in bright, filtered shade; this understory epiphyte needs no soil and colors best with slightly brighter indirect light while still avoiding harsh direct sun.

directions: Tillandsia flabellata produces a broad, flattened, fan-shaped flower spike of overlapping bright red to orange-red bracts held above a rosette of soft green, arching leaves — a wider, more distinctly fan-like bract structure than the narrower spikes of T. multicaulis or T. capitata. Native to the mountain forests of Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras, it grows as a shaded epiphyte in cloud-forest conditions with high humidity and filtered light. Small violet flowers emerge sequentially from the fan of bracts, extending the colorful display over several weeks. It benefits from more frequent misting than desert-adapted tillandsias and should never receive intense direct sun, which quickly bleaches the leaves.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Tillandsia flabellata species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water, flushing monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Guzmania zahnii is distinguished by a rosette of long, glossy leaves that twist gently in a loose spiral around the central axis, giving it a more dynamic, corkscrewed silhouette than the flatter rosettes of G. lingulata or G. musaica. From the center rises a tall, narrow, torch-like spike of overlapping bracts in shades of orange, red, and yellow, topped with small white flowers, and the spiral leaf arrangement remains visible even when the plant is not in bloom. Native to the cloud forests of Costa Rica and Panama, it is one of the more shade-tolerant Guzmania species and performs well as a low-light indoor or lanai plant. Keep the central cup filled with water and grow in bright indirect light for the best leaf color and spike display.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Guzmania zahnii species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water, flushing monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Guzmania conifera earns its name from a tightly packed, cone-shaped inflorescence of overlapping orange-and-yellow bracts that closely resembles a small pinecone, a noticeably different bloom architecture than the flattened or open torch spikes of most Guzmania species already in this collection. The dense, glossy green leaves form a broad rosette below the cone, native to the humid mountain forests of Colombia and Ecuador. Small white flowers peek from between the bracts of the cone over several weeks. It is well suited to deep indoor shade or a shaded lanai, tolerating lower light than most flowering houseplants, and should be kept with water standing in its central cup at all times.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Guzmania conifera species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water, flushing monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Guzmania wittmackii produces an upright, branching spike of vivid red-orange to salmon bracts from which noticeably larger, showy white flowers open one at a time — the flowers are far more conspicuous and long-lasting than the tiny, mostly hidden blossoms of G. lingulata or G. sanguinea. The soft, mid-green, strap-shaped leaves form an open rosette typical of tank bromeliads, native to the rainforests of Ecuador, Peru, and Colombia. This species has been an important parent in many commercial Guzmania hybrids because of its bright bract color and prominent flowers. Grow in bright indirect shade with the central cup kept filled, and expect the bract display to remain colorful for two to three months.

planting.note: Grow as a large specimen container plant in zone 10-12 shade; pot in a coarse, well-draining bark mix, since a mature rosette can span several feet and takes years to reach flowering size.

directions: Vriesea gigantea lives up to its name as one of the largest species in the genus, forming a massive rosette of broad, arching leaves marked with irregular dark green to purplish-brown checkering and blotching — a bolder, larger-scale mottling than the fine banding of V. fenestralis or the striping of V. splendens. A mature plant can take several years to reach flowering size before sending up a tall, branched, candelabra-like spike of yellow-green bracts and flowers well above the foliage. Native to the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil, it is grown primarily as a dramatic specimen accent for large shaded beds or containers rather than a compact houseplant. Its size and slow growth make it a long-term investment piece in a shade garden.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Vriesea gigantea species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water, flushing monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Vriesea platynema has broad, wine-purple to maroon banding across its wide, arching leaves, producing a horizontally striped effect similar in concept to but coarser and more purple-toned than the maroon banding of V. splendens. Its tall, branched flower spike bears yellow bracts tinged with red at the base, rising well above the leaf rosette on a stiff, upright stalk. Native to Brazil and found in both epiphytic and terrestrial forms in the wild, it adapts readily to potted container culture. Because it tolerates a wider range of light than the deep-shade V. hieroglyphica, it can be grown in moderate to bright indirect light for the most vivid leaf banding.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Vriesea platynema species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water, flushing monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Vriesea psittacina gets its common name of Parrot Vriesea from an inflorescence that combines green, yellow, and scarlet-red segments along a single branched spike, resembling the colorful plumage of a parrot — a multicolor effect distinct from the single-tone red spike of V. splendens or the yellow-and-red of V. carinata. The plain green leaf rosette is smaller and more compact than many Vriesea species, keeping the focus on the flamboyant bloom. Native to the coastal forests of Brazil, it is a smaller, easier-to-place species for tabletop or shaded shelf display than the giant tank-forming Vrieseas. It blooms readily in cultivation and the color display persists for one to two months.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Vriesea psittacina species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water, flushing monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Vriesea saundersii forms a low, flat, spreading rosette of thick, silvery-gray leaves speckled and mottled with purple-maroon spots on both surfaces, especially vivid on the leaf undersides — a stiffer, more succulent-textured foliage than the soft, glossy leaves of V. splendens or V. fenestralis. Its low, flattened growth habit and thicker leaves reflect an origin in drier, more exposed rocky habitats of southeastern Brazil compared to the humid forest floor species in the genus. A branched spike of yellow flowers with green bracts rises modestly above the foliage. Because of its tougher, more drought-tolerant leaves, it needs less frequent watering than most other Vriesea species and tolerates brighter light without leaf scorch.

common_name: Ampullacea Neoregelia (Urn Bromeliad, Spotted Tube Bromeliad)

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or mounted on bark in bright indirect shade; the trailing, tubular habit shows best when allowed to cascade rather than grown upright in a standard pot.

directions: Neoregelia ampullacea is a small, trailing species that forms narrow, tubular, urn-shaped rosettes on wiry stolons, creeping and cascading rather than forming the flat, cartwheel-like rosette typical of N. carolinae or N. spectabilis. The slender leaves are marked with irregular maroon spotting and banding, more pronounced in brighter light, and the plant is best displayed in a hanging basket or mounted on a slab where its trailing stems can drape freely. Small violet flowers appear deep within each tubular rosette. Native to the coastal forests of Brazil, it spreads readily by stolons and makes an easy groundcover-style bromeliad for shaded hanging displays.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Neoregelia ampullacea species profile

planting.note: Grow as a shaded container or coastal landscape accent in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water.

directions: Neoregelia cruenta gets its common name Blood Bromeliad from the intense, saturated crimson-red blush that spreads across the entire center of the rosette at bloom time — a deeper, more solidly saturated red than the more localized center blush of N. carolinae. The stiff, spine-edged, gray-green leaves form a wide, flat rosette adapted to the sandy coastal dune habitats of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, where the species grows in full exposure to salt spray and bright light. Small violet flowers form in the water-filled central tank. Because of its coastal dune origin, it tolerates more direct sun, wind, and salt exposure than most shade-loving Neoregelia species.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Neoregelia cruenta species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water for best color development.

directions: Neoregelia 'Royal Burgundy' is a long-established hybrid whose entire flat rosette of leaves emerges and stays deep wine-red to burgundy from base to tip, in contrast to species like N. carolinae that stay green except for a seasonal center blush confined to the inner leaves. The uniform, all-over color intensifies in brighter indirect light and remains attractive year-round rather than fading after a single bloom cycle. Small pale blue-violet flowers form in the central tank when the plant matures. Because the color is a consistent foliage trait rather than a temporary bloom response, it provides steady dark color in a shaded bed or container display throughout the year.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water.

directions: Neoregelia marmorata has broad, olive-green leaves overlaid with irregular purple-maroon blotches and marbling scattered across the entire leaf surface, a mottled, marble-like pattern distinct from the solid center blush of N. carolinae or the fine spotting of N. ampullacea. The wide, flat rosette is typical of the genus, native to the Atlantic Forest region of Brazil, and the marbled pattern intensifies with brighter indirect light. Small lavender flowers appear in the water-holding central cup at maturity. Its irregular, painterly foliage pattern makes it a popular parent species in ornamental Neoregelia breeding programs aimed at mottled and marbled leaf forms.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water.

directions: Aechmea nudicaulis produces its flower spike on a strikingly bare, naked stalk rising well clear of the leaves before opening into orange-red bracts with small yellow flowers — the tall, leafless flower stem is the feature the species name refers to and sets it apart from the shorter, leaf-nestled spikes of A. fasciata or A. gamosepala. The stiff, spine-edged, yellow-green leaves banded with darker cross-striping form a wide, tank-forming rosette typical of Aechmea. Widely distributed from Mexico through the Caribbean into South America, it is one of the most common and adaptable Aechmea species in cultivation. It tolerates a broad range of light and humidity conditions better than many showier hybrid Aechmeas.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Aechmea nudicaulis species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water.

directions: Aechmea orlandiana has broad, olive-green leaves boldly cross-banded with irregular chocolate-maroon to near-black blotches in a zebra-like pattern, a much more strongly patterned leaf than the silvery cross-banding of A. fasciata or the smooth green of A. gamosepala. Its low, spreading rosette is smaller and more compact than many tank-forming Aechmeas, making it well suited to windowsill or shaded tabletop culture. A short, dense spike of pink bracts with small yellow flowers rises just above the leaves. Native to Brazil, its dramatic leaf patterning rather than its flowers is the primary ornamental feature, and pattern intensity increases with brighter indirect light.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; pot in a well-draining bark mix and keep the central tank filled with water.

directions: Aechmea weilbachii forms a narrow, upright, smooth-leaved rosette without spines, sending up a tall, slender spike of soft pink bracts studded with small violet-blue flowers — a more delicate, spineless, upright form than the broader, spine-edged rosettes of A. chantinii or A. nudicaulis. The plain green leaves lack the banding or blotching seen in many other Aechmea species, keeping visual attention on the elegant pink-and-blue flower spike. Native to the coastal rainforests of Brazil, it grows as an epiphyte in filtered light. Its smooth, spineless leaves make it easier to handle and site near walkways than more heavily armed Aechmea species.

planting.note: Grow as a terrestrial clumping accent in a shaded bed or large container in zone 9b-12; this cold-hardier Aechmea tolerates brief light frost better than most tank bromeliads once established.

directions: Aechmea distichantha is a large, vigorously clumping, mostly terrestrial species that spreads into substantial colonies rather than remaining a single specimen rosette like A. fasciata or A. chantinii. Stiff, spine-edged, gray-green leaves surround a dense, branched inflorescence of rose-pink to purple bracts with small violet-blue flowers, giving rise to the common name Heart of Flame Bromeliad. Widely distributed from Brazil and Bolivia south into Argentina, it grows in more open, sun-exposed habitats than most shade-loving Aechmeas and is noted among bromeliad growers as one of the more cold-tolerant species in the genus, handling brief exposure to near-freezing temperatures once mature. Its clumping habit and greater sun and cold tolerance make it a useful mass-planted accent in marginal outdoor zone 9b-10 landscapes.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Aechmea distichantha species profile
